front.text: Intelligence at the Edge of Every Disaster
A Resilient, AI-Powered Environmental Intelligence Network
Complete Project Document — Architecture, Hardware, AI/ML, Deployment and Feasibility
Team Members: Kasula Kiran, K.S.V.Dheeraj Kumar, B.Ram Charan Reddy, M.Divya Tejswi, Ch.Jishnu Chowdary, K.Sai Sahitya Kannam

blocks.text: India faces recurring, high-impact environmental hazards: urban and river floods across Assam, Bihar, Kerala and Maharashtra; forest fires across Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and central India; hazardous air pollution in major cities; landslides in hill states; and industrial gas/chemical incidents. Government agencies such as NDMA, IMD and ISRO already run environmental monitoring and early-warning systems, but these are largely centralized and coarse-grained. They lack dense, hyperlocal, real-time, offline-capable sensing at the exact point of risk.

EcoShield is a distributed, AI-powered Environmental Intelligence Network built around a Universal Node Platform with field-replaceable, hazard-specific sensor pods. Each node performs on-device (edge) AI to detect anomalies locally. Nodes connect over LoRaWAN to an edge gateway, which performs advanced multi-sensor fusion, camera-based vision AI, and risk assessment — continuing to operate even when internet connectivity fails. Only critical alerts, summaries and risk assessments are transmitted onward to cloud infrastructure and, ultimately, to regional control centres and national dissemination systems such as NDMA's SACHET and C-DOT's CAP-based alerting.
Core Design Pipeline: Sense → Verify → Fuse → Predict → Decide → Alert → Act → Learn

The system is explicitly designed to complement — not replace — India's existing monitoring and dissemination ecosystem (IMD, CWC, FSI, CPCB, ISRO, SACHET/C-DOT). EcoShield's contribution is the missing layer: continuous, distributed, evidence-fused, offline-resilient local sensing and decision-making, feeding validated intelligence upward into systems that already reach the public at national scale.

items: A single Universal Node hardware core that is reconfigured for any hazard by swapping a sensor pod — not five different products.
Automatic pod identification and AI-profile loading — no firmware reflash needed when a pod is changed.
Risk (severity) and Confidence are computed and reported as two separate values, not collapsed into one number.
Quorum-Gated Alerting: a public CRITICAL alert requires corroboration from at least two independent evidence sources, which also functions as the system's core anti-spoofing defence.
Trust-weighted neighbour recalibration, grounded in published wireless-sensor-network research, so a drifting sensor is corrected rather than simply ignored.
A full offline-first emergency path — local detection, local voice/siren alerting, and store-and-forward buffering — that keeps working with zero internet connectivity.

A five-layer security spine (signed identity, encrypted transport, physical-plausibility checks, quorum-gated fusion, tamper/audit logging) defending against cloned nodes, replay attacks and spoofed readings.

blocks.text: Problem Statement ID: 26178  |  Sponsor: Qualcomm Inc.  |  Category: Hardware  |  Theme: Disaster Management.

Official title: “A resilient, AI-powered environmental monitoring network that provides early detection, localized intelligence, and actionable alerts for floods, forest fires, pollution events, and other environmental hazards common in India, enabling authorities and communities to shift from reactive disaster response to proactive risk prevention.”

The description calls for a distributed Environmental Intelligence Network deployable across cities, rivers, forests, industrial zones and vulnerable communities, using on-device AI, multi-hazard early warning, regional risk mapping, community/authority notification, a cloud-edge hybrid architecture, and scalable, cost-effective deployment.

Hazardous air pollution — major urban centres.
Landslides and terrain instability — hill and slope regions.
Industrial gas leaks and chemical incidents — industrial zones and plant perimeters.
Water quality degradation and extreme heat/weather — as advanced deployment extensions.

sections.title: 3. Existing Ecosystem and the Genuine Gap

blocks.text: EcoShield is designed to complement, not replace, India's existing monitoring and alerting infrastructure. The genuine gap it targets is the combination of distributed local sensing, on/near-device intelligence, sensor-health awareness, multi-sensor and neighbour evidence fusion, offline resilience, and actionable geo-targeted risk intelligence — not the absence of any single government system.

blocks.text: 3.1 Case Study: Kerala 2018 Floods and CAP Dissemination

Kerala's official Orange Book of Disaster Management records that C-DOT's Common Alerting Protocol-compliant platform, integrated with telecom providers for geo-targeted SMS, was used to send up to 11.4 lakh precautionary messages during the 2018 floods. This is strong evidence that the dissemination problem can be solved operationally at scale — but it is evidence of dissemination capability, not of field-level hazard detection. EcoShield is designed to feed richer, earlier, evidence-backed alert events into exactly this kind of dissemination infrastructure.
Note: Quantitative figures such as the 11.4 lakh message count are historical (2018) and should be labelled with their time period; C-DOT's platform has since evolved.

EcoShield is an evidence-fused, edge-first, resilient environmental intelligence platform. It senses multiple hazards, verifies sensor reliability, fuses local and external evidence, detects and assesses risk at the edge, and delivers resilient, multi-channel alerts even when cloud connectivity is unavailable.

items: Local intelligence first — critical decisions never depend on continuous cloud connectivity.
Evidence over single-sensor triggers — one abnormal reading never automatically becomes a public disaster alert.
Risk and confidence are treated as separate dimensions, not one blended score.
Sensor health is itself a form of environmental intelligence.
One common node platform serves every deployment environment through modular sensor pods and AI profiles.
The network complements existing government and institutional systems rather than claiming to replace them.
Advanced features are part of the target architecture, but all prototype claims are limited to what is actually built and measured.
Human authorities remain responsible for final safety decisions and operational actions — the system is decision support, not autonomous control.

Critical extreme event: a deterministic safety override can bypass normal evidence-gathering delay when a reading is far beyond any plausible danger threshold.

blocks.text: EXTERNAL INTELLIGENCE (Weather / Satellite / Existing Systems) feeds into the Node layer alongside direct sensing. Universal Nodes (sensor pods, sensor health, local baseline, trend/anomaly detection, safety rules, buffering) send data over LoRaWAN to the Edge Gateway (multi-node fusion, advanced ML, camera/thermal AI, risk + confidence engine, local alerts, offline operation). The gateway forwards over 4G/5G/Wi-Fi to the Cloud/Regional Control Centre (GIS, history, training, forecasting, digital twin, fleet and model registry), which in turn feeds the CAP/SACHET alert ecosystem (SMS, voice, cell broadcast, app, radio, TV, web).

The hardware design deliberately favours widely available, inexpensive, well-documented components so that a student team can source, wire and validate a full working prototype without specialised equipment. Every component listed below is commercially available in India at the time of writing; exact prices should be re-verified before purchase.

blocks.text: Recommendation: build one Universal Core with both sensor pods and physically swap the pod during the live demonstration, rather than building two entirely separate nodes. This is both cheaper and a stronger proof of the modularity claim than two static units.

items: Weekend 1 — establish ESP32-S3 to Wio-E5 UART communication; send and receive a test LoRa packet on the gateway. Confirms the communications backbone before any sensor work.
Weekend 2 — wire and validate Hydro pod sensors individually; confirm sane readings; integrate into firmware with a CUSUM-based persistence check.
Weekend 3 — wire and validate Fire/Air pod sensors; integrate the node-level fire-score logic; build the pod-identification mechanism.

blocks.text: The node is designed as a rugged, field-hardware version of plug-and-play modularity: a Universal Core that never changes, combined with hazard-specific Sensor Pods that can be added, removed or replaced. This is deliberately “LEGO-like” in principle but industrial-grade in execution — keyed, locking, weatherproof, vibration-resistant connectors, not consumer-toy connectors.

items: Each sensor pod carries its own small identity/calibration memory chip (a low-cost I2C EEPROM), storing pod type, model, measurement range, unit, calibration coefficients and driver/firmware compatibility.
The moment a pod is connected, the node reads this chip over the shared I2C bus and instantly knows what is attached — no manual configuration.
The node matches the identity against an internal Pack Registry (a lookup table) mapping pod type to sensor drivers, AI model file, and alert thresholds.
It then automatically initializes the correct drivers, loads the matching pre-trained AI model from flash storage, applies calibration coefficients, and reports READY status to the dashboard.
No firmware reflash is required — the same physical node becomes a Flood node, Fire node or Air-Quality node purely based on which pod is attached.

blocks.text: Hot-swapping is explicitly not claimed as a safety feature, since outdoor sensors are exposed to moisture, static discharge, and electrical transients that make live swapping unsafe. Instead, the platform uses a controlled Maintenance Mode sequence:

Maintenance Mode → isolate sensor interface → remove old/failed pod → insert replacement pod → identify pod metadata → self-test → calibration/health validation → load driver + AI profile → return to service.

items: Sensor replacement — same pod type, e.g. a broken PM sensor pod swapped for a new one of the same type.
Sensor expansion — adding an additional pod to an existing node, e.g. a flood node gaining a water-quality pod.
Mission reconfiguration — changing what the node monitors entirely, e.g. a forest fire node relocated and reconfigured as an industrial gas node.

blocks.text: Because the expensive components (MCU, radio, battery system, enclosure) remain with the Universal Core, a maintenance team only needs to carry spare pods rather than entire spare nodes — significantly simplifying field logistics at scale.

sections.title: 8. Sensor, Node, Gateway, Network and System Health

blocks.text: Health monitoring is treated as a first-class intelligence dimension, not an afterthought. The platform must be able to distinguish a real environmental event from a failing sensor, degraded node, communication problem or power problem — and it must never let equipment failure masquerade as an environmental disaster.

blocks.text: Unhealthy sensors are down-weighted or excluded from evidence fusion according to configured rules, rather than being silently trusted. Maintenance alerts are generated for calibration overdue, battery degradation, repeated sensor faults, communication deterioration, and tamper events. The fleet dashboard displays health and environmental risk as separate views so an operator can immediately distinguish “high hazard” from “unreliable node.”

blocks.text: Note: Mesh self-healing (a node automatically re-associating with the nearest live gateway if its primary gateway fails) is listed as a ROADMAP feature only. It is not claimed as a working prototype capability unless the reassociation logic is actually implemented and tested.

The AI architecture is deliberately distributed across three tiers with distinct responsibilities — not three copies of the same model. Model selection throughout is benchmark-driven: a simpler model is preferred whenever it matches or beats a more complex one on measured precision, recall, false-alarm rate, latency, memory and energy.

Signal processing chain: raw sensor reading → range/plausibility check → Median/Hampel filter (spike removal) → EWMA/Kalman smoothing → rate-of-change and acceleration features → CUSUM sustained-shift detection → quantized TinyML logistic classifier → deterministic safety override for extreme values.

CUSUM formula: Cₜ = max(0, Cₜ₋₁ + (xₜ − baseline − k)); an anomaly is flagged when Cₜ exceeds a configured threshold h. This detects a sustained shift in sensor readings while remaining robust to single-sample noise.
10.2 AI-1 — Qualcomm/Edge Gateway Intelligence (primary environmental intelligence layer)

items: Isolation Forest — unsupervised anomaly scoring, chosen because real disaster-event labels are naturally sparse and imbalanced.
XGBoost — separate supervised hazard classifiers per hazard type (Flood-XGB, Fire-XGB, Pollution-XGB, Landslide-XGB); efficient enough to run on CPU, no NPU required.
GRU — short-horizon escalation forecasting (e.g. predicted water level 10 minutes ahead); benchmarked against LSTM and simple lag-feature baselines rather than assumed superior.
Explicit spatial-graph features — neighbour_mean_risk, upstream/downstream gradient, agreement ratio — used instead of a full graph neural network in the prototype.

RTMDet → MobileNetV3-Small — a compact vision detector identifies a smoke/flame region of interest, and a lightweight verifier classifies the cropped region; both models are supported on Qualcomm AI Hub for the IQ-8275 target.

blocks.text: 10.3 AI-2 — Cloud/Regional Intelligence (not on the emergency path)

items: Model training, calibration and validation on larger historical datasets.
GAT/GraphSAGE and temporal-GNN research for advanced hazard-propagation modelling — explicitly an advanced research direction, not a prototype prerequisite.
Digital twin and what-if simulation.
Fleet analytics, drift monitoring, and a versioned model registry with rollback.

blocks.text: E = Σ(wᵢ · eᵢ) / Σ(wᵢ), where wᵢ = base_reliabilityᵢ × data_qualityᵢ × freshnessᵢ × relevanceᵢ.

Every evidence source — a sensor reading, a neighbouring node's corroboration, weather context, or camera evidence — is dynamically weighted rather than treated equally. A stale, low-quality or historically unreliable source contributes proportionally less to the final risk assessment.

The architecture deliberately uses heterogeneous compute rather than assuming every model must run on an AI accelerator: XGBoost and Isolation Forest run efficiently on general-purpose CPU; GRU, RTMDet and MobileNetV3-Small use the NPU; image preprocessing uses the ISP/GPU where available. On the Raspberry Pi prototype, all models run on CPU; NPU placement is the documented production plan for the Qualcomm Dragonwing IQ-8275.
10.6 Detection vs. Forecasting — an Honest Distinction

A single low-cost node with only its own sensors can realistically perform anomaly/threshold detection — recognizing that something unusual is happening right now at its location. Genuine multi-hour forecasting (e.g. “75% chance of flooding in 3 hours”) requires broader context: data from multiple nodes across a basin, historical patterns, and often external rainfall forecasts. EcoShield therefore places detection at the node (AI-0) and short-to-medium horizon forecasting at the gateway and cloud tiers (AI-1/AI-2), where that broader context is actually available.
11.1 Risk and Confidence as Separate Dimensions

rows: Unusual trend or early evidence; insufficient corroboration for a public warning
Multiple evidence sources support an active/developing hazard
Strong evidence and/or severe, rapidly escalating conditions
Multi-channel emergency alert + authority escalation + local warning

blocks.text: Confidence (LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH) is computed and displayed independently of severity. A “CRITICAL / MEDIUM confidence” state is an intentional, explainable possibility — a potentially severe reading that lacks full independent corroboration is not the same as a “HIGH / HIGH confidence” event that is strongly supported by multiple sources. This separation is deliberately kept visible on the dashboard as a live two-axis (quadrant) view rather than collapsed into a single number.

A CRITICAL public alert requires corroboration from at least two independent evidence sources (for example, two sensors on the same node, a neighbouring node, or camera confirmation), or an extreme, deterministic safety-override threshold. This single design rule serves two purposes simultaneously: it is the escalation logic that prevents false public alarms from a single noisy sensor, and it is the system's core defence against a single spoofed or compromised node fabricating a disaster.

The camera is treated strictly as a gateway-side visual module, not a LoRa sensor. Raw video is never transmitted over LoRaWAN — the link's bandwidth simply cannot carry it, and attempting to do so would defeat the purpose of a low-power sensor network.

items: Capture — RGB (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3) and optionally thermal (FLIR Lepton 3.5 / MLX90640) frames at the gateway.

Vision inference — RTMDet detects a smoke/flame region of interest; MobileNetV3-Small verifies the cropped region.
Evidence extraction — detection class, confidence, timestamp, location, bounding box, model version.
Multimodal fusion — visual evidence combined with PM, gas, temperature, humidity, neighbour and weather evidence.
Upstream transmission — compact event metadata by default; a compressed snapshot or short clip is uploaded only for high-confidence events, via 4G/5G/Wi-Fi — never LoRaWAN.
Offline mode — the gateway continues vision inference, fusion and local alerting even when backhaul fails; selected evidence is buffered for later synchronization.

blocks.text: Flood nodes follow the hydrological path rather than an arbitrary grid, using four positional classes:

items: Upstream node — earliest detection of a rising water event.
River/channel node — tracks the main flow.
Downstream node — confirms progression toward vulnerable areas.
Vulnerable-zone node — placed directly at the community or infrastructure at risk.

blocks.text: This upstream → channel → downstream → vulnerable-zone chain allows the system to measure the spatial progression of a flood wave and warn downstream nodes before the water arrives, rather than relying on a single absolute water-level reading.
Security is treated as a full defence-in-depth spine, where each layer defends against a specific, named attack rather than a generic “we have security” claim.

blocks.text: Residents can confirm what they are observing via a simple IVR keypress or app action. This human corroboration feeds directly into the confidence score alongside sensor and camera evidence, closing the loop between the automated network and the people who actually live in the affected area.

Alert status progresses through generated → delivered → acknowledged → resolved. Unacknowledged CRITICAL events automatically escalate to the next configured authority level. Full audit logs preserve alert and acknowledgement history.

The Alert Engine includes a CAP Bridge that converts an approved internal event into a Common Alerting Protocol-compliant message — hazard type, severity, certainty/confidence representation, location/geometry, effective time, expiry, instruction, and language fields. Internal rich evidence (raw sensor values, model scores, node health, fusion trace) is kept separate from the public alert payload, but every public alert references its originating event ID and model/rule version for full auditability. EcoShield positions itself explicitly as complementing SACHET/C-DOT dissemination infrastructure, not replacing or rebuilding it.

The platform can surface rule-based, safety-reviewed suggested actions (e.g. monitor a downstream flood zone, verify a fire-affected area, inspect a bridge, issue an air-quality advisory). This layer is explicitly decision support — it does not autonomously issue unsafe operational commands.

blocks.text: The digital twin is a what-if simulation layer (e.g. “simulate 200mm rainfall over this basin in 6 hours”) used for planner decision support and scenario testing. It is explicitly treated as an advanced, cloud-side capability rather than a headline feature or a prerequisite for the core working prototype, since equivalent functionality is commonly claimed by many competing systems.
Node density and placement are not based on a simplistic rule such as “one node every X metres.” Instead, placement follows a combined optimisation:
Risk Map + Hazard Map + Population + Critical Infrastructure + Terrain + Radio Coverage → Node Placement Optimisation.

items: High-risk areas receive denser and/or redundant sensing.
Low-risk areas use sparser coverage.
Critical locations can have independent redundant sensors to improve corroboration.
Placement aims to maximise useful evidence, not simply maximise node count.

blocks.text: Large deployments are divided into local gateway zones, each serving a cluster of nearby nodes. Critical zones can use overlapping gateway coverage so that loss of a single gateway does not eliminate local sensing. The resilience claim is explicitly edge decision-making plus local buffering plus retry/store-and-forward — a custom self-healing mesh is not claimed unless actually implemented and tested.

blocks.text: Wherever possible, sensor pods are retrofitted onto existing infrastructure — electricity poles, telecom towers, and CWC gauge stations — instead of constructing new greenfield sites. This sharply reduces installation cost, time, and land/permission overhead.
17.5 Economic Framing: Cost per km² of Coverage

Rather than presenting only a raw per-node bill of materials, deployment economics are framed as cost per km² of previously unmonitored coverage gained — turning the hardware cost table into an impact argument rather than a parts list.

Field maintenance and labour logistics across remote, climatically diverse terrain.

Class imbalance in training data, since real disaster events are naturally rare.
Ridge-line gateway placement, directional antennas, and redundant gateway coverage in critical zones.
Store-and-forward buffering plus a local voice/siren failsafe independent of gateway/cloud availability; the gateway's own SIM provides a backup voice/SMS/IVR path even without broadband.
Trust-weighted neighbour recalibration turns sensor drift into a self-correcting network property instead of a maintenance emergency.
The five-layer security spine directly defends against spoofing and cloned-node attacks; no single compromised node can trigger a public CRITICAL alert.

A two-tier labour model: local caretakers (aligned with Panchayat/Jal Jeevan Mission networks) handle basic upkeep, while regional technicians perform pod-level field replacement, guided by remote health telemetry so visits are planned rather than reactive.
A CAP-compatible payload is built and demonstrated now, with live SACHET/C-DOT integration explicitly positioned as an authorized deployment step rather than a prototype dependency.
Weighted losses, event-based evaluation, and careful negative sampling address class imbalance honestly rather than through synthetic overfitting.

blocks.text: Rural and urban communities in flood-prone (Assam, Bihar, Kerala, Maharashtra), fire-prone (Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, central India) and industrially exposed regions gain earlier, localized, offline-resilient warnings — shifting disaster response from reactive to proactive. Human Confirm Alerts and multilingual offline voice ensure the system reaches people without smartphones or reliable data connectivity. Government agencies (NDMA, IMD, ISRO, state SDMAs) gain a dense, hyperlocal evidence layer that strengthens their existing forecasting and dissemination infrastructure rather than duplicating it.
21.2 Impact Metrics (Design Targets — Pending Field Validation)

items: Minutes-level local detection versus approximately 3 hours for satellite-based fire detection (NASA FIRMS MODIS/VIIRS); satellites can miss short-lived fires entirely between overpasses.
Reduced false-alarm rate via quorum-gated, multi-sensor and neighbour-corroborated alerting versus single-sensor triggers.
Zero dependency on cloud connectivity for the local emergency alerting path.
Deployment cost reduction via infrastructure-piggyback siting versus greenfield installation.
Scalable from a single node (~₹9,000–12,500) to district/state coverage without redesigning hardware.
Eight distinct failure modes explicitly handled with a defined system response, not just the happy path.

blocks.text: Faster, localized, spoof-resistant warnings save lives in remote and low-connectivity areas. Multilingual offline voice and IVR-based Human Confirm Alerts include populations that smartphone-app-based systems structurally leave behind.

Substantially lower cost than expanding reference-grade infrastructure (a single CPCB monitoring station costs ₹50 lakh or more). Infrastructure-piggyback siting and cost-per-km²-of-coverage framing make network expansion economically defensible. Earlier, better-verified action reduces downstream disaster response and relief costs.

E-waste-sourced camera modules reduce both electronic waste and hardware cost simultaneously. Better forest-fire, pollution and water-quality monitoring directly supports conservation and public-health policy. Solar-powered, low-maintenance nodes minimize the network's own environmental footprint.

sections.title: 25. Anticipated Jury Questions and Prepared Answers

items: Why does the node need AI if the gateway has more compute? — The node's AI-0 layer exists to keep the emergency detection and local-alert path functional with zero connectivity to the gateway or cloud; it performs filtering, plausibility checks and a lightweight anomaly signal so the network degrades gracefully rather than going blind.

Why not send all data directly to the cloud? — LoRaWAN payloads are extremely small by design to keep power consumption low; continuous raw streaming is neither technically possible over this link nor necessary, since most value comes from summarized, evidence-fused decisions rather than raw time-series.

Why can't LoRa carry camera video? — LoRa payloads are measured in bytes, not kilobytes; a single video frame is orders of magnitude too large. This is precisely why the camera connects directly to the gateway rather than routing through a node's LoRa radio.

How do you distinguish a faulty sensor from a real hazard? — Every reading passes through sensor-health scoring (plausibility, temporal consistency, calibration state) and is checked against neighbouring nodes; an isolated abnormal reading without corroboration is flagged as a sensor anomaly rather than promoted to a public alert.

How do you prevent a false alarm from one sensor? — Quorum-Gated Alerting requires at least two independent evidence sources, or a deterministic extreme-value override, before any CRITICAL public alert is issued.

How does the system work without internet? — The edge gateway performs the full risk/confidence calculation and issues local voice/siren alerts entirely offline; events are buffered locally and synchronized once connectivity returns.

What happens when a sensor pod is replaced? — The new pod's identity chip is read automatically, the correct driver and AI profile are loaded, and the node completes a self-test and calibration check before returning to service — no firmware reflash is required.

What data trains your models? — A combination of public institutional datasets (CWC, IMD, CPCB, NASA FIRMS, NASA Global Landslide Catalog) for baseline features and labels, and the team's own controlled bench and field data for calibration and fine-tuning; these sources are always clearly distinguished in reporting.

How do you evaluate false negatives and false positives? — Using location-aware and time-aware train/test splits to avoid leakage, and reporting precision, recall, F1, false-positive rate, false-negative rate, detection latency and lead time for every candidate model before selection.

What is simulated versus physically demonstrated? — The physical prototype demonstrates two real field nodes, one gateway, live pod-swap reconfiguration, offline/reconnect behaviour, and evidence-fused alerting; district/state-scale deployment, live SACHET integration, and a full digital twin are explicitly simulated or represented as standards-compatible interfaces rather than claimed as fully built.

Is a large language model making the safety decision? — No. Generative AI is restricted to natural-language dashboard queries, human-readable explanations of why an alert was raised, and report summarization. It is never the primary hazard detector and does not independently decide whether a critical event exists.
